answer key scores them mechanically.

Your case must be **hard but fair**. A careful analyst who reads only the initial
file should be likely to get the central question wrong or leave it unresolved.
A careful analyst who collects the right one to three catalogue items should be able
to answer every item correctly and defend each answer from the evidence alone.

- Case id: `OD2-DEV-OBVWRONG`
- Split: `dev`

- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.

Each expected answer is what a careful analyst would conclude after reading the
initial file **plus the optimal read path** (at most three catalogue items, which you
name in `optimalReadPath`). For classes INCOMPLETE and NOCONC, the expected answer is
what the **whole catalogue** supports. For the leading question that is "unknown",
and SUFF is "insufficient" unless no intervention is warranted.

## Rules

   domain trivia beyond what a competent generalist knows. If two answers are

2. Traps must be fair: every misleading signal is countered by specific evidence in
   the initial file or the catalogue.
3. No source type is automatically authoritative. Leaders, staff, logs, dashboards,
   vendors and experts may each be right, wrong, interested, or gamed.
4. Include at least one item whose correct answer is "unknown" or "association-only",
   and at least one action that is "premature".
5. Do not mention EDF, Clarity, Kepner-Tregoe, or any named diagnostic framework or
   method. Do not use the phrases "root cause", "origin network", "control point",
   "propagation", "IS / IS NOT", "five whys", or "fishbone".
6. Catalogue titles say what would be collected, never what it shows. Bad: "Logs
   showing the cache bug". Good: "Application error logs, 1–14 March".
7. Distractor catalogue items must be things a reasonable analyst might request.
8. Everything is fictional. Do not name or closely reconstruct a real organization,

    most three items.
13. Evidence citations: `requiredEvidence` lists the items needed to justify the

Return one JSON object with two members, `case` and `truth`, through the structured

`case`:
```
{ "id", "split", "benchmarkClass", "domain", "title", "setting", "presentingRequest",
  "initialEvidence": [{"id","stage","source","sourceType","text"}],
  "catalogue": [{"id","stage","title","source","sourceType","text"}],
  "candidates": {"hypotheses":[{"id","text"}], "edges":[{"id","from","to","relation"}], "actions":[{"id","text"}]},

- allowedAnswers: hypothesis ["supported","contradicted","unknown"]; edge
  ["causal","association-only","contradicted","unknown"]; action
  ["preferred","acceptable","premature","harmful"]; sufficiency

case.title: Larkmoor Parks: the maintenance overtime overrun
case.setting: The Larkmoor Parks and Open Space Department (fictional) maintains parks in four districts: Riverside, Eastgate, Millbrook and Summit Hill. The maintenance division has 112 maintenance-worker positions. This year the city adopted several budget reductions, including a citywide hiring freeze from 6 January. Maintenance overtime for April–September is well over budget, and the council's Finance Committee wants an explanation and a corrective plan.
case.presentingRequest: The Budget Office has asked you to explain the overtime overrun in the parks maintenance division and recommend what the department should do before the Finance Committee deadline of 15 December. The Director believes the hiring freeze is the cause and has asked for an exemption to fill eleven positions.

initialEvidence.source: Office of Budget & Management memo to the Parks Director
initialEvidence.text: Re: Overtime variance, April–September. Parks maintenance overtime for April–September totals $688,400, compared with $412,100 for the same months last year (+67%) and a budget of $430,000. Council's Finance Committee has asked for an explanation and corrective plan by 15 December. For reference, this year's adopted reductions for the department were: citywide hiring freeze on non-public-safety positions (from 6 January); deferral of two mower replacements ($118,000); non-renewal of the after-hours closing services contract ($96,000); reduced seasonal temp hours ($40,000). Please route your response through this office.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Director Ruth Okafor-Lind, 3 November
initialEvidence.text: 'This is the hiring freeze, plain and simple. We started the year six maintenance workers short and we're at seventeen now. Every vacancy is a route somebody has to cover after their shift. July was brutal too, because the heat meant extra irrigation checks and mowing catch-up. I've asked the City Manager for an exemption to fill eleven positions; that brings overtime back to normal within a quarter.' Asked about other drivers, she said the closing contract 'was a small line, crews absorbed it.' She said she had not seen a breakdown of overtime by pay code.

initialEvidence.source: HR/payroll extract prepared at the Director's request
initialEvidence.text: Maintenance division, current year. Month: vacant maintenance-worker positions (of 112) / overtime paid. Jan 6 / $52.3k; Feb 8 / $49.1k; Mar 10 / $55.0k; Apr 12 / $104.2k; May 15 / $109.0k; Jun 17 / $118.1k; Jul 17 / $121.4k; Aug 17 / $119.3k; Sep 17 / $116.4k. HR analyst note: correlation between monthly vacancies and monthly overtime, January–September, r = 0.93. 'Overtime has tracked the vacancy count closely all year.'

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Dale Visconti, crew lead, Millbrook district, 5 November
initialEvidence.text: 'We're running routes two and three people short. Guys are holding over an hour or two most days to finish mowing. On top of that, since spring we're back out at night a few times a week, and nobody's seen their kids in months. Morale is the lowest I've seen in nineteen years. If they'd just fill the positions this would sort itself out.' He estimated he personally had worked 'about 25 hours of overtime a month' since April.

initialEvidence.source: City Ethics Hotline intake record #2611
initialEvidence.text: Received 22 August from an anonymous caller identifying as a parks employee. Allegation: two Riverside maintenance workers (named in the sealed record as Employees R-14 and R-22) 'are claiming night call-backs for parks they never go to. It's all paper slips, nobody checks. They're each pulling an extra grand a month.' Caller declined follow-up contact. Status: referred to Internal Audit for review on 26 August.

initialEvidence.source: Email from the Municipal Employees Local 418 steward to the Director, 7 November
initialEvidence.text: Members are exhausted and grievances are coming. Two points. First, in Eastgate the night lock-ups keep going to the same handful of people the supervisor likes, and others never get asked. Second, if management answers this with an overtime cap, understand that members will stop taking call-backs, and then the gates and restrooms don't get locked. Nobody wants a repeat of the splash-pad break-in two years ago. Fill the vacancies and treat people fairly.

initialEvidence.source: Risk Management quarterly summary, parks maintenance
initialEvidence.text: Workers' compensation claims filed April–September: 15 (prior year, same period: 9). Claim types: strains/sprains 8, lacerations 3, slips/falls 3, other 1. Lost workdays: 112 (prior: 61). Safety coordinator's note: 'The rise coincides with heavy overtime; fatigue is a likely factor and we recommend a review.' No analysis of hours worked by individual claimants has been performed.

catalogue.title: City Manager hiring-freeze directive and citywide exemption log
catalogue.text: Directive 2026-01 freezes all non-public-safety hiring from 6 January until further notice. Departments may request exemptions for positions 'essential to health, safety, or legally mandated service.' Exemption log to date: 9 requests citywide, 4 approved (all in the water utility and 911 dispatch). Parks submitted one request on 28 October for 11 maintenance-worker positions; it is pending. The directive does not restrict overtime or contract spending.

catalogue.title: Regional weather station summary, April–September, current and prior year
catalogue.text: Days at or above 35°C: 6 (prior year 2). Mean July high 31.8°C (prior 30.1°C). April–September rainfall 388 mm (prior 402 mm). Growing-season degree days +4%. All four parks districts lie within 9 km of the station; no district-level variation is recorded.

catalogue.title: Budget office overtime workbook by pay code and district, April–September, current and prior year
catalogue.source: Office of Budget & Management, payroll analytics
catalogue.text: April–September, prior year → current year. By pay code: OT-X holdover $341.0k → $358.1k (hours +1.5%; rest reflects the 3.5% July wage increase); CB call-back $38.2k → $289.3k; other (holiday, storm, event) $32.9k → $41.0k. By district: total OT, call-back portion, and vacant positions at 30 September. Riverside $112k → $205k, CB $10k → $95k, 5 of 30 vacant. Eastgate $104k → $200k, CB $9k → $98k, 1 of 30 vacant. Millbrook $98k → $179k, CB $9k → $84k, 6 of 28 vacant. Summit Hill $98k → $104k, CB $10k → $12k, 5 of 24 vacant. Call-back entries: 2,295 (prior 312); 1,962 carry task code CLOSE (prior 0), all dated 1 April or later, none in Summit Hill; other call-backs 333. Data aggregated by district; no employee-level detail.

catalogue.title: Workers' compensation claim log, parks maintenance, April–September
catalogue.text: Fifteen claims. Each entry lists date, time of injury, task and injury type; the district field is blank on most entries. 11 of 15 injuries occurred between 07:00 and 13:00; 9 involved mowing, trimming or lifting. The claim form does not record hours worked in the preceding 24 hours or whether the employee had worked a call-back the previous night, and payroll records have not been matched to claims. The prior-year log shows a similar task mix (6 of 9 involved mowing, trimming or lifting).

catalogue.title: Collective agreement excerpts, Articles 12 and 14 (overtime and call-back)
catalogue.text: Art. 12.3: work beyond the scheduled 8-hour shift is paid at 1.5× in 15-minute increments. Art. 12.7: management may not change regular shift start times without 30 days' notice and consultation. Art. 14.1: an employee recalled to work after leaving the worksite receives a minimum of three hours' pay at 1.5×, regardless of time worked. Art. 14.4: call-back is voluntary unless no volunteer is available, in which case the least-senior qualified employee is directed. Wage schedule: 3.5% increase effective 1 July.

catalogue.title: Procurement file for the after-hours closing services contract, with related operational memo
catalogue.source: Purchasing Division file PK-2219; Deputy Director memo of 24 March
catalogue.text: Contract PK-2219 with Kestrel Night Services covered nightly closing of gates, restrooms and splash pads at 41 sites in Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook for $96,000 a year. It expired 31 March and was not renewed (adopted budget reduction). Summit Hill's 12 sites are closed under a separate contract paid by the Summit Hill Business Improvement District, which continued unchanged. Memo, Deputy Director Paul Senanayake, 24 March: 'From 1 April, nightly closing at the 41 sites will be done by maintenance staff on call-back under Art. 14. Supervisors will post sign-up sheets. Closing is a condition of the city's liability coverage and must not be skipped.' Margin note: 'Net saving est. $60k after modest OT.'

catalogue.title: HR exit interview summaries, maintenance workers separating January–September
catalogue.text: Eleven separations (8 resignations, 3 retirements). Primary reasons cited by those who resigned: higher pay elsewhere (5), commute or relocation (2), conflict with a supervisor (1). Three mentioned 'too much overtime' as a secondary reason. Under the hiring freeze, no position was backfilled.

catalogue.title: Interview with the Eastgate district supervisor
catalogue.source: Interview notes, Marisol Adeyemi-Clark, Eastgate supervisor, 10 November
catalogue.text: 'I post a sign-up sheet every Monday for the week's closings. The same five or six people sign up most nights, because others have childcare or second jobs. If nobody signs, I direct the junior person, like the contract says. I don't keep the old sheets; they go in the bin when the week's over.' She said no one had told her about a complaint. She declined to estimate how call-backs were split among her 29 staff.

catalogue.title: Internal Audit memo on hotline intake #2611
catalogue.text: Auditors matched 120 call-back claims (April–August) against electronic gate-controller and restroom smart-lock event logs, including all 64 claims by Employees R-14 and R-22. For 117 of 120 claims (and 64 of 64 for R-14 and R-22), the logs show lock events at the claimed sites within 40 minutes of the claimed time. The three exceptions were at sites without smart locks, and supervisor sign-off sheets confirm attendance. Conclusion: no evidence of claims for work not performed. Observation: under the 3-hour minimum, each 30–45 minute closing round is paid as three hours.

catalogue.title: Recreation division event permit summary, April–September
catalogue.text: Athletic field and pavilion permits issued: 1,284 (prior year 1,236, +4%). Events requiring staff attendance after 18:00: 61 (prior 58). Tournament weekends: 14 (prior 13). Event staffing overtime is charged to the Recreation cost center under pay code EV, not to the maintenance division.

catalogue.title: Fleet maintenance log for parks mowers and utility vehicles, January–September
catalogue.text: Both mowers whose replacement was deferred remained in service. Unplanned mower downtime: 47 unit-days (prior year 39). Longest outage: 9 days (Riverside, June). On 6 occasions, work orders note that crews 'doubled up on remaining units.' No vehicle downtime affecting evening or night operations was recorded.

catalogue.title: Regional parks benchmarking survey: overtime share of maintenance payroll, prior fiscal year
catalogue.text: Eight comparable municipalities. Overtime as a share of maintenance payroll: median 7.2%, range 4.1%–11.8%. Larkmoor, prior year: 6.9%. Figures are self-reported and the survey does not break out pay codes. Current-year figures have not yet been collected.

hypotheses.text: The overtime increase is driven mainly by maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze, with crews working extra hours to cover open routes.
The overtime increase is driven mainly by nightly closing duties moved onto maintenance staff as 3-hour-minimum call-backs after the after-hours closing contract was not renewed.
Padded or fictitious call-back claims account for a material share of the overtime increase.
Extra irrigation and mowing work caused by the hot summer is a main driver of the overtime increase.
In Eastgate, the supervisor is steering lock-up call-backs to a favored subset of staff.

edges.from: Rise in maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze
edges.to: Rise in maintenance overtime spending, April–September

edges.from: Non-renewal of the after-hours closing contract for Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook
edges.to: Rise in call-back overtime in those three districts

edges.from: Higher overtime hours among maintenance staff
edges.to: Rise in workers' compensation injury claims

actions.text: Restore contracted nightly closing for the 41 Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook sites (through an emergency extension or a re-tender, mirroring the Summit Hill arrangement), and track call-back spending against the April–September level.
Impose an immediate department-wide cap of 12 overtime hours per worker per month.
Refer Employees R-14 and R-22 for disciplinary investigation and suspend their call-back eligibility in the meantime.
Remove the Eastgate supervisor from call-back scheduling and issue her a written reprimand for favoritism.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: The overrun is real: April–September maintenance overtime rose by $276k. The hiring freeze is not what drove it. Holdover overtime (OT-X), the pay code that would capture crews covering vacant routes, rose only 1.5% in hours. Almost all of the increase (+$251k) is call-back pay, and 1,962 of those entries carry the new CLOSE task code, starting on 1 April. On that date the $96k after-hours closing contract for the 41 sites in Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook expired. The Deputy Director reassigned nightly closing to maintenance staff on call-back. Under the labor agreement, each 30–45 minute closing round pays three hours at time-and-a-half. Summit Hill makes a natural contrast. Its closing contract is paid by a business improvement district and continued. It has the joint-highest vacancy rate (21%), yet its overtime rose only 6%. Eastgate, with 3% vacancies, saw overtime rise 92%. The vacancy–overtime correlation in the HR extract is confounded: vacancies rose in the same months that the closing duty arrived. Internal Audit matched the hotline-named workers' claims to electronic lock logs, so padding is ruled out. The Eastgate favoritism allegation can't be resolved because sign-up sheets aren't kept and payroll data is aggregated. case.title: Larkmoor Parks: the maintenance overtime overrun
case.setting: The Larkmoor Parks and Open Space Department (fictional) maintains parks in four districts: Riverside, Eastgate, Millbrook and Summit Hill. The maintenance division has 112 maintenance-worker positions. This year the city adopted several budget reductions, including a citywide hiring freeze from 6 January. Maintenance overtime for April–September is well over budget, and the council's Finance Committee wants an explanation and a corrective plan.
case.presentingRequest: The Budget Office has asked you to explain the overtime overrun in the parks maintenance division and recommend what the department should do before the Finance Committee deadline of 15 December. The Director believes the hiring freeze is the cause and has asked for an exemption to fill eleven positions.

initialEvidence.source: Office of Budget & Management memo to the Parks Director
initialEvidence.text: Re: Overtime variance, April–September. Parks maintenance overtime for April–September totals $688,400, compared with $412,100 for the same months last year (+67%) and a budget of $430,000. Council's Finance Committee has asked for an explanation and corrective plan by 15 December. For reference, this year's adopted reductions for the department were: citywide hiring freeze on non-public-safety positions (from 6 January); deferral of two mower replacements ($118,000); non-renewal of the after-hours closing services contract ($96,000); reduced seasonal temp hours ($40,000). Please route your response through this office.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Director Ruth Okafor-Lind, 3 November
initialEvidence.text: 'This is the hiring freeze, plain and simple. We started the year six maintenance workers short and we're at seventeen now. Every vacancy is a route somebody has to cover after their shift. July was brutal too, because the heat meant extra irrigation checks and mowing catch-up. I've asked the City Manager for an exemption to fill eleven positions; that brings overtime back to normal within a quarter.' Asked about other drivers, she said the closing contract 'was a small line, crews absorbed it.' She said she had not seen a breakdown of overtime by pay code.

initialEvidence.source: HR/payroll extract prepared at the Director's request
initialEvidence.text: Maintenance division, current year. Month: vacant maintenance-worker positions (of 112) / overtime paid. Jan 6 / $52.3k; Feb 8 / $49.1k; Mar 10 / $55.0k; Apr 12 / $104.2k; May 15 / $109.0k; Jun 17 / $118.1k; Jul 17 / $121.4k; Aug 17 / $119.3k; Sep 17 / $116.4k. HR analyst note: correlation between monthly vacancies and monthly overtime, January–September, r = 0.93. 'Overtime has tracked the vacancy count closely all year.'

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Dale Visconti, crew lead, Millbrook district, 5 November
initialEvidence.text: 'We're running routes two and three people short. Guys are holding over an hour or two most days to finish mowing. On top of that, since spring we're back out at night a few times a week, and nobody's seen their kids in months. Morale is the lowest I've seen in nineteen years. If they'd just fill the positions this would sort itself out.' He estimated he personally had worked 'about 25 hours of overtime a month' since April.

initialEvidence.source: City Ethics Hotline intake record #2611
initialEvidence.text: Received 22 August from an anonymous caller identifying as a parks employee. Allegation: two Riverside maintenance workers (named in the sealed record as Employees R-14 and R-22) 'are claiming night call-backs for parks they never go to. It's all paper slips, nobody checks. They're each pulling an extra grand a month.' Caller declined follow-up contact. Status: referred to Internal Audit for review on 26 August.

initialEvidence.source: Email from the Municipal Employees Local 418 steward to the Director, 7 November
initialEvidence.text: Members are exhausted and grievances are coming. Two points. First, in Eastgate the night lock-ups keep going to the same handful of people the supervisor likes, and others never get asked. Second, if management answers this with an overtime cap, understand that members will stop taking call-backs, and then the gates and restrooms don't get locked. Nobody wants a repeat of the splash-pad break-in two years ago. Fill the vacancies and treat people fairly.

initialEvidence.source: Risk Management quarterly summary, parks maintenance
initialEvidence.text: Workers' compensation claims filed April–September: 15 (prior year, same period: 9). Claim types: strains/sprains 8, lacerations 3, slips/falls 3, other 1. Lost workdays: 112 (prior: 61). Safety coordinator's note: 'The rise coincides with heavy overtime; fatigue is a likely factor and we recommend a review.' No analysis of hours worked by individual claimants has been performed.

catalogue.title: City Manager hiring-freeze directive and citywide exemption log
catalogue.text: Directive 2026-01 freezes all non-public-safety hiring from 6 January until further notice. Departments may request exemptions for positions 'essential to health, safety, or legally mandated service.' Exemption log to date: 9 requests citywide, 4 approved (all in the water utility and 911 dispatch). Parks submitted one request on 28 October for 11 maintenance-worker positions; it is pending. The directive does not restrict overtime or contract spending.

catalogue.title: Regional weather station summary, April–September, current and prior year
catalogue.text: Days at or above 35°C: 6 (prior year 2). Mean July high 31.8°C (prior 30.1°C). April–September rainfall 388 mm (prior 402 mm). Growing-season degree days +4%. All four parks districts lie within 9 km of the station; no district-level variation is recorded.

catalogue.title: Budget office overtime workbook by pay code and district, April–September, current and prior year
catalogue.source: Office of Budget & Management, payroll analytics
catalogue.text: April–September, prior year → current year. By pay code: OT-X holdover $341.0k → $358.1k (hours +1.5%; rest reflects the 3.5% July wage increase); CB call-back $38.2k → $289.3k; other (holiday, storm, event) $32.9k → $41.0k. By district: total OT, call-back portion, and vacant positions at 30 September. Riverside $112k → $205k, CB $10k → $95k, 5 of 30 vacant. Eastgate $104k → $200k, CB $9k → $98k, 1 of 30 vacant. Millbrook $98k → $179k, CB $9k → $84k, 6 of 28 vacant. Summit Hill $98k → $104k, CB $10k → $12k, 5 of 24 vacant. Call-back entries: 2,295 (prior 312); 1,962 carry task code CLOSE (prior 0), all dated 1 April or later, none in Summit Hill; other call-backs 333. Data aggregated by district; no employee-level detail.

catalogue.title: Workers' compensation claim log, parks maintenance, April–September
catalogue.text: Fifteen claims. Each entry lists date, time of injury, task and injury type; the district field is blank on most entries. 11 of 15 injuries occurred between 07:00 and 13:00; 9 involved mowing, trimming or lifting. The claim form does not record hours worked in the preceding 24 hours or whether the employee had worked a call-back the previous night, and payroll records have not been matched to claims. The prior-year log shows a similar task mix (6 of 9 involved mowing, trimming or lifting).

catalogue.title: Collective agreement excerpts, Articles 12 and 14 (overtime and call-back)
catalogue.text: Art. 12.3: work beyond the scheduled 8-hour shift is paid at 1.5× in 15-minute increments. Art. 12.7: management may not change regular shift start times without 30 days' notice and consultation. Art. 14.1: an employee recalled to work after leaving the worksite receives a minimum of three hours' pay at 1.5×, regardless of time worked. Art. 14.4: call-back is voluntary unless no volunteer is available, in which case the least-senior qualified employee is directed. Wage schedule: 3.5% increase effective 1 July.

catalogue.title: Procurement file for the after-hours closing services contract, with related operational memo
catalogue.source: Purchasing Division file PK-2219; Deputy Director memo of 24 March
catalogue.text: Contract PK-2219 with Kestrel Night Services covered nightly closing of gates, restrooms and splash pads at 41 sites in Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook for $96,000 a year. It expired 31 March and was not renewed (adopted budget reduction). Summit Hill's 12 sites are closed under a separate contract paid by the Summit Hill Business Improvement District, which continued unchanged. Memo, Deputy Director Paul Senanayake, 24 March: 'From 1 April, nightly closing at the 41 sites will be done by maintenance staff on call-back under Art. 14. Supervisors will post sign-up sheets. Closing is a condition of the city's liability coverage and must not be skipped.' Margin note: 'Net saving est. $60k after modest OT.'

catalogue.title: HR exit interview summaries, maintenance workers separating January–September
catalogue.text: Eleven separations (8 resignations, 3 retirements). Primary reasons cited by those who resigned: higher pay elsewhere (5), commute or relocation (2), conflict with a supervisor (1). Three mentioned 'too much overtime' as a secondary reason. Under the hiring freeze, no position was backfilled.

catalogue.title: Interview with the Eastgate district supervisor
catalogue.source: Interview notes, Marisol Adeyemi-Clark, Eastgate supervisor, 10 November
catalogue.text: 'I post a sign-up sheet every Monday for the week's closings. The same five or six people sign up most nights, because others have childcare or second jobs. If nobody signs, I direct the junior person, like the contract says. I don't keep the old sheets; they go in the bin when the week's over.' She said no one had told her about a complaint. She declined to estimate how call-backs were split among her 29 staff.

catalogue.title: Internal Audit memo on hotline intake #2611
catalogue.text: Auditors matched 120 call-back claims (April–August) against electronic gate-controller and restroom smart-lock event logs, including all 64 claims by Employees R-14 and R-22. For 117 of 120 claims (and 64 of 64 for R-14 and R-22), the logs show lock events at the claimed sites within 40 minutes of the claimed time. The three exceptions were at sites without smart locks, and supervisor sign-off sheets confirm attendance. Conclusion: no evidence of claims for work not performed. Observation: under the 3-hour minimum, each 30–45 minute closing round is paid as three hours.

catalogue.title: Recreation division event permit summary, April–September
catalogue.text: Athletic field and pavilion permits issued: 1,284 (prior year 1,236, +4%). Events requiring staff attendance after 18:00: 61 (prior 58). Tournament weekends: 14 (prior 13). Event staffing overtime is charged to the Recreation cost center under pay code EV, not to the maintenance division.

catalogue.title: Fleet maintenance log for parks mowers and utility vehicles, January–September
catalogue.text: Both mowers whose replacement was deferred remained in service. Unplanned mower downtime: 47 unit-days (prior year 39). Longest outage: 9 days (Riverside, June). On 6 occasions, work orders note that crews 'doubled up on remaining units.' No vehicle downtime affecting evening or night operations was recorded.

catalogue.title: Regional parks benchmarking survey: overtime share of maintenance payroll, prior fiscal year
catalogue.text: Eight comparable municipalities. Overtime as a share of maintenance payroll: median 7.2%, range 4.1%–11.8%. Larkmoor, prior year: 6.9%. Figures are self-reported and the survey does not break out pay codes. Current-year figures have not yet been collected.

hypotheses.text: The overtime increase is driven mainly by maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze, with crews working extra hours to cover open routes.
The overtime increase is driven mainly by nightly closing duties moved onto maintenance staff as 3-hour-minimum call-backs after the after-hours closing contract was not renewed.
Padded or fictitious call-back claims account for a material share of the overtime increase.
Extra irrigation and mowing work caused by the hot summer is a main driver of the overtime increase.
In Eastgate, the supervisor is steering lock-up call-backs to a favored subset of staff.

actions.text: Restore contracted nightly closing for the 41 Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook sites (through an emergency extension or a re-tender, mirroring the Summit Hill arrangement), and track call-back spending against the April–September level.

Refer Employees R-14 and R-22 for disciplinary investigation and suspend their call-back eligibility in the meantime.

case.title: Larkmoor Parks: the maintenance overtime overrun
case.setting: The Larkmoor Parks and Open Space Department (fictional) maintains parks in four districts: Riverside, Eastgate, Millbrook and Summit Hill. The maintenance division has 112 maintenance-worker positions. This year the city adopted several budget reductions, including a citywide hiring freeze from 6 January. Maintenance overtime for April–September is well over budget, and the council's Finance Committee wants an explanation and a corrective plan.
case.presentingRequest: The Budget Office has asked you to explain the overtime overrun in the parks maintenance division and recommend what the department should do before the Finance Committee deadline of 15 December. The Director believes the hiring freeze is the cause and has asked for an exemption to fill eleven positions.

initialEvidence.source: Office of Budget & Management memo to the Parks Director
initialEvidence.text: Re: Overtime variance, April–September. Parks maintenance overtime for April–September totals $688,400, compared with $412,100 for the same months last year (+67%) and a budget of $430,000. Council's Finance Committee has asked for an explanation and corrective plan by 15 December. For reference, this year's adopted reductions for the department were: citywide hiring freeze on non-public-safety positions (from 6 January); deferral of two mower replacements ($118,000); non-renewal of the after-hours closing services contract ($96,000); reduced seasonal temp hours ($40,000). Please route your response through this office.

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Director Ruth Okafor-Lind, 3 November
initialEvidence.text: 'This is the hiring freeze, plain and simple. We started the year six maintenance workers short and we're at seventeen now. Every vacancy is a route somebody has to cover after their shift. July was brutal too, because the heat meant extra irrigation checks and mowing catch-up. I've asked the City Manager for an exemption to fill eleven positions; that brings overtime back to normal within a quarter.' Asked about other drivers, she said the closing contract 'was a small line, crews absorbed it.' She said she had not seen a breakdown of overtime by pay code.

initialEvidence.source: HR/payroll extract prepared at the Director's request
initialEvidence.text: Maintenance division, current year. Month: vacant maintenance-worker positions (of 112) / overtime paid. Jan 6 / $52.3k; Feb 8 / $49.1k; Mar 10 / $55.0k; Apr 12 / $104.2k; May 15 / $109.0k; Jun 17 / $118.1k; Jul 17 / $121.4k; Aug 17 / $119.3k; Sep 17 / $116.4k. HR analyst note: correlation between monthly vacancies and monthly overtime, January–September, r = 0.93. 'Overtime has tracked the vacancy count closely all year.'

initialEvidence.source: Interview notes, Dale Visconti, crew lead, Millbrook district, 5 November
initialEvidence.text: 'We're running routes two and three people short. Guys are holding over an hour or two most days to finish mowing. On top of that, since spring we're back out at night a few times a week, and nobody's seen their kids in months. Morale is the lowest I've seen in nineteen years. If they'd just fill the positions this would sort itself out.' He estimated he personally had worked 'about 25 hours of overtime a month' since April.

initialEvidence.source: City Ethics Hotline intake record #2611
initialEvidence.text: Received 22 August from an anonymous caller identifying as a parks employee. Allegation: two Riverside maintenance workers (named in the sealed record as Employees R-14 and R-22) 'are claiming night call-backs for parks they never go to. It's all paper slips, nobody checks. They're each pulling an extra grand a month.' Caller declined follow-up contact. Status: referred to Internal Audit for review on 26 August.

initialEvidence.source: Email from the Municipal Employees Local 418 steward to the Director, 7 November
initialEvidence.text: Members are exhausted and grievances are coming. Two points. First, in Eastgate the night lock-ups keep going to the same handful of people the supervisor likes, and others never get asked. Second, if management answers this with an overtime cap, understand that members will stop taking call-backs, and then the gates and restrooms don't get locked. Nobody wants a repeat of the splash-pad break-in two years ago. Fill the vacancies and treat people fairly.

initialEvidence.source: Risk Management quarterly summary, parks maintenance
initialEvidence.text: Workers' compensation claims filed April–September: 15 (prior year, same period: 9). Claim types: strains/sprains 8, lacerations 3, slips/falls 3, other 1. Lost workdays: 112 (prior: 61). Safety coordinator's note: 'The rise coincides with heavy overtime; fatigue is a likely factor and we recommend a review.' No analysis of hours worked by individual claimants has been performed.

catalogue.text: Directive 2026-01 freezes all non-public-safety hiring from 6 January until further notice. Exemption log to date: 9 requests citywide, 4 approved (all in the water utility and 911 dispatch). Parks submitted one request on 28 October for 11 maintenance-worker positions; it is pending. The directive does not restrict overtime or contract spending.

catalogue.text: Days at or above 35°C: 6 (prior year 2). Mean July high 31.8°C (prior 30.1°C). April–September rainfall 388 mm (prior 402 mm). Growing-season degree days +4%. All four parks districts lie within 9 km of the station; no district-level variation is recorded.

catalogue.text: Eleven separations (8 resignations, 3 retirements). Primary reasons cited by those who resigned: higher pay elsewhere (5), commute or relocation (2), conflict with a supervisor (1). Three mentioned 'too much overtime' as a secondary reason. Under the hiring freeze, no position was backfilled.

The three exceptions were at sites without smart locks, and supervisor sign-off sheets confirm attendance. Conclusion: no evidence of claims for work not performed. Observation: under the 3-hour minimum, each 30–45 minute closing round is paid as three hours.

actions.text: Restore contracted nightly closing for the 41 Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook sites (through an emergency extension or a re-tender, mirroring the Summit Hill arrangement), and track call-back spending against the April–September level.
Impose an immediate department-wide cap of 12 overtime hours per worker per month.
Refer Employees R-14 and R-22 for disciplinary investigation and suspend their call-back eligibility in the meantime.
Remove the Eastgate supervisor from call-back scheduling and issue her a written reprimand for favoritism.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: The overrun is real: April–September maintenance overtime rose by $276k. The hiring freeze is not what drove it. Holdover overtime (OT-X), the pay code that would capture crews covering vacant routes, rose only 1.5% in hours. Almost all of the increase (+$251k) is call-back pay, and 1,962 of those entries carry the new CLOSE task code, starting on 1 April. On that date the $96k after-hours closing contract for the 41 sites in Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook expired. The Deputy Director reassigned nightly closing to maintenance staff on call-back. Under the labor agreement, each 30–45 minute closing round pays three hours at time-and-a-half. Summit Hill makes a natural contrast. Its closing contract is paid by a business improvement district and continued. It has the joint-highest vacancy rate (21%), yet its overtime rose only 6%. Eastgate, with 3% vacancies, saw overtime rise 92%. The vacancy–overtime correlation in the HR extract is confounded: vacancies rose in the same months that the closing duty arrived. Internal Audit matched the hotline-named workers' claims to electronic lock logs, so padding is ruled out. The Eastgate favoritism allegation can't be resolved because sign-up sheets aren't kept and payroll data is aggregated. The rise in injuries co-occurs with the overtime, but nothing links the two at the individual level. Restoring contracted closing is the fix the evidence supports.

answers.rationale: The initial file fits the vacancy story perfectly (r = 0.93, Director and crew lead agree). C3 refutes it. Holdover hours, which is where vacancy coverage shows up, rose only 1.5%. Summit Hill has a 21% vacancy rate but only +6% overtime, while Eastgate has 3% vacancies and +92% overtime. Nearly all of the increase is CLOSE-coded call-backs. The correlation comes from timing: vacancies rose in the same months the closing duty arrived.

C6 shows the closing contract for 41 sites ended on 31 March and the duty moved to call-back from 1 April. C3 shows call-back pay up $251k of the $276k total increase, 1,962 CLOSE entries (none the year before) all from 1 April onward, and none in Summit Hill, where the BID contract continued. The overtime step in E3 begins in April. C9 and C5 confirm that each short closing round is paid as three hours.

Internal Audit matched 117 of 120 sampled call-back claims, and all 64 claims by the two named workers, to electronic lock events at the claimed sites and times. The three exceptions were confirmed by supervisor sign-off. The call-back cost reflects the 3-hour minimum, not fictitious claims.

Extra irrigation or mowing would show up as holdover hours or non-closing call-backs. Holdover hours rose 1.5%, and non-CLOSE call-backs went from 312 to 333 entries. Summit Hill had the same weather and flat overtime. The hot July (C2) is real but does not explain the increase.

The allegation comes from the steward. C3 is aggregated by district and has no employee-level detail. Even C8 is consistent with self-selection by volunteers (voluntary call-back under C5), and the sign-up sheets are discarded. No item discriminates, so the claim is live but unestablished.

Across districts, vacancies and overtime growth do not move together: the highest-vacancy district (Summit Hill) is flat and the lowest-vacancy district (Eastgate) nearly doubled. Holdover hours barely changed. The time-series correlation is explained by the April closing reassignment happening at the same time.

The order in time fits: the contract lapsed on 31 March and CLOSE call-backs start on 1 April. The memo documents the mechanism, and Art. 14's 3-hour minimum sets the pay. The effect appears only in the three districts that lost the contract. Summit Hill, which kept its contract and has high vacancies, serves as a control. The main rival explanation, vacancies, is ruled out by the same contrast.

Claims (9 to 15) and overtime rose over the same period, and the safety coordinator suspects fatigue. No one has matched injured workers to the hours they worked or to call-backs the night before (E7, and C4 confirms the data does not exist). Causation is not established and nothing refutes it.

This directly reverses the mechanism. The old contract cost $96k a year, against roughly $250k of extra call-back pay in six months. Summit Hill shows that contracted closing keeps call-back pay flat. It also preserves the closing duty required by the liability insurer.

Call-back is voluntary (C5), and the steward warns that members would stop taking lock-ups. Nightly closing is a condition of the liability coverage (C6), and there was a prior break-in. A cap would leave sites unlocked and would not address the contract lapse that drives the cost.
The audit verified all 64 claims by R-14 and R-22 against the lock logs. Disciplining them punishes workers who did the work, and suspending them also reduces the pool of closing volunteers.
This could be right if favoritism were confirmed (H5), but H5 is unknown. Nothing establishes that call-backs are being steered rather than self-selected, so a reprimand is not justified yet.

The pay-code breakdown, the procurement record and the Summit Hill contrast together establish the driver and its mechanism well enough to commit to restoring contracted closing. The questions still open (favoritism, injuries) do not bear on that decision.

truth.authoringNotes: Obvious diagnosis: hiring-freeze vacancies (Director, crew lead, r = 0.93 table). The contrast case is Summit Hill (highest vacancies, flat overtime) against Eastgate (lowest vacancies, +92%), together with the pay-code split in C3. The less salient cause, the closing contract dropped as a $96k 'saving', is flagged fairly in the initial file: E1 lists it, E2 dismisses it, E3 shows a step change in April, E4 mentions night work 'since spring', and E6 mentions lock-ups. The padding trap (E5) is resolved by C9. The favoritism allegation (E6) is deliberately unresolvable: no catalogue item gives employee-level distribution, which makes A4 premature. The injury edge stays association-only even after C4, because the claim form lacks hours data and C4's district field is blank, so C4 offers no contrast. C5 and C8 are relevant but do not change any answer; they are left off both lists. Numbers reconcile: pay codes 341.0+38.2+32.9=412.1 and 358.1+289.3+41.0=688.4; districts 112+104+98+98=412 and 205+200+179+104=688; call-back 10+9+9+10=38 and 95+98+84+12=289; vacancies 5+1+6+5=17; E3 April–September monthly totals sum to 688.4; 6 vacancies in January plus 11 separations = 17.
